title: Gut-training: the impact of two weeks repetitive gut-challenge during exercise on gastrointestinal status, glucose availability, fuel kinetics, and running performance
authors: Costa RJS, Miall A, Khoo A, Rauch C, Snipe R, Camoes-Costa V, Gibson P
population: Endurance runners (n = 25); gut-challenge trial of 2 h running at 60% VO2max with 30 g CHO (2:1 glucose/fructose) gel-disc every 20 min plus 1 h distance test, then 2 weeks of gut-training and a repeat trial
findings: Participants randomised to carbohydrate gel-disc (CHO-S), carbohydrate food (CHO-F) or placebo (PLA) for 2 weeks of repetitive gut-challenge.
GI symptoms fell by 60% (p = 0.008) on CHO-S and 63% (p = 0.046) on CHO-F, reductions greater than PLA (p < 0.05).
Peak breath H2 (malabsorption marker) lower after CHO-S (6 ppm) than CHO-F (9) and PLA (12); blood glucose higher on CHO-S (7.2 vs 6.1 and 6.2 mmol/L).
1 h distance test improved 5.2% (CHO-S) and 4.3% (CHO-F) but not PLA (-2.1%) (p = 0.009).
No differences in oxidation rates, plasma I-FABP or cortisol.
limitations: Small trial (n = 25 across three arms), 2-week intervention, 60 g/h challenge, laboratory-style running, not ultra-distance; the abstract does not state the number or frequency of training sessions in the intervention.
implications: A 2-week repeated gut-challenge block is supported before a key long effort; trial challenge used about 2 h at 60% VO2max with ~60 g CHO/h (30 g every 20 min). Session frequency is not stated in the abstract, so do not claim an evidence-based session count from this paper.
Gut-training works with gels or real-food CHO; log a GI symptom score after each session to titrate dose.
Describe performance benefit only as 'possible' (single small trial).

verification.notes: Crossref match; every number re-checked against the Europe PMC abstract. Removed the researcher's '2-3 long runs' implication because the abstract does not state session frequency.
